'''Malcolm John Perry''' (born 13 November 1951) is a British [[theoretical physics|theoretical physicist]] and [[emeritus]] professor of theoretical physics at [[University of Cambridge]] and professor of theoretical physics at [[Queen Mary University of London]]. His research mainly concerns [[quantum gravity]], [[black hole]]s, [[general relativity]], and [[supergravity]].

==Biography==
Perry attended [[King Edward's School, Birmingham]], before reading physics at [[St John's College, Oxford]]. He was a graduate student at [[King's College, Cambridge]], under the supervision of [[Stephen Hawking]]. He obtained his doctorate in 1978 with a thesis on the quantum mechanics of black holes. In these early years, he worked on several very influential papers on [[Euclidean quantum gravity]] and [[black hole radiation]] with [[Gary Gibbons]] and Hawking.<ref>
{{Cite journal |last1=Gibbons |first1=G. W |author-link=Gary Gibbons |last2=Hawking |first2=S. W |author-link2=Stephen Hawking |last3=Perry |first3=M. J |year=1978 |title=Path Integrals and the Indefiniteness of the Gravitational Action |journal=Nucl. Phys. |volume=B 138 |issue=1 |pages=141–150 |bibcode=1978NuPhB.138..141G |doi=10.1016/0550-3213(78)90161-X}}</ref>

After his graduate studies, he worked in [[Princeton, New Jersey]], from 1978 to 1986. With his student Rob Myers, he found the [[higher-dimensional Einstein gravity|Myers–Perry metric]], which describes the higher-dimensional generalization of the [[Kerr metric]].<ref>{{cite journal| title = Black Holes in Higher Dimensional Space-Times | journal = Annals of Physics | volume = 172| issue = 2| pages = 304–347| year = 1986| doi = 10.1016/0003-4916(86)90186-7 |bibcode = 1986AnPhy.172..304M | last1 = Myers | first1 = Robert C. | last2 = Perry | first2 = M. J }}</ref> He also started working on [[supergravity]], [[string theory]] and [[Kaluza–Klein theory]].<ref>{{cite journal| title = Magnetic Monopoles in Kaluza-Klein Theories|author = [[David Gross|David J. Gross]], Malcolm J. Perry| journal = Nucl. Phys. B|volume = 226| issue = 1| pages = 29–48| year = 1983| doi = 10.1016/0550-3213(83)90462-5     
|bibcode = 1983NuPhB.226...29G }}</ref> In his final years in Princeton he worked with [[Curtis Callan]], [[Emil Martinec]] and [[Daniel Friedan]] to calculate the low-energy effective action for string theory.<ref>{{cite journal| title = Strings in background fields| author = [[Curtis Callan|Curtis Callan Jr.]], [[Emil Martinec|Emil J. Martinec]], [[Daniel Friedan]], Malcolm J. Perry| journal = Nucl. Phys. B 
|volume = 262| issue = 4| pages = 593–609| year = 1985| doi = 10.1016/0550-3213(85)90506-1
|bibcode = 1985NuPhB.262..593C}}</ref>

In 1986, he returned to [[Cambridge]], being elected a fellow of [[Trinity College, Cambridge]], where he has worked ever since. In 2010, his attention has focused on [[Generalized complex structure|generalised geometry]] and the doubled formalism for [[string theory]], extending these ideas to M-theory in collaboration with David Berman.<ref>{{cite journal| title = Generalized geometry and M theory|author1=David Berman |author2=Malcolm J. Perry | journal = JHEP| volume = 1106| issue = 6| pages = 74| year = 2011| doi = 10.1007/JHEP06(2011)074 |arxiv = 1008.1763 |bibcode = 2011JHEP...06..074B |s2cid=118482271 }}</ref> In 2016, he returned to black hole physics with Hawking and [[Andrew Strominger]] and began a series of highly influential works attempting to solve long standing problems in black hole thermodynamics.
